meta.blurb: A dirty, tired seventeen-year-old walks into Philadelphia with almost no money, buys three rolls and is laughed at by a girl who will become his wife. Benjamin Franklin tells the rest himself, from his thirteen virtues to the clubs he founded.
meta.bible: Benjamin Franklin: born in Boston in January 1706, died in 1790 aged 84; printer, writer, inventor, public servant; the author, who wrote the book in parts in 1771, 1784 and 1788 and left it unfinished. William Franklin: his son, to whom the first part is addressed as Dear Son. Josiah Franklin: his father, a Candle and Soap maker from Ecton in Northamptonshire. Abiah Folger: his mother. James Franklin: his older brother, a printer, who made Benjamin his apprentice at twelve. John Collins: a boyhood friend. Matthew Adams: a bookseller's customer who lent him books. Silence Dogood: the made-up widow in whose name Benjamin wrote letters to his brother's newspaper. Samuel Keimer: a printer in Philadelphia. Sir William Keith: the governor of Pennsylvania, who promised letters of credit and sent none. James Ralph: a friend who sailed with him to London. Thomas Denham: a kind Quaker merchant. Hugh Meredith: his first business partner. Deborah Read: his wife from 1730. Joseph Breintnall, Thomas Godfrey, Robert Grace, William Coleman: members of the Junto, the club of friends. George Whitefield: the preacher of 1739. Dr Thomas Bond: his friend who began the hospital. General Edward Braddock: the British commander of 1755. Pennsylvania Gazette: his newspaper from 1729. Poor Richard: the Almanack he published from 1732. Library Company: the first subscription library, 1731. Pilgrim's Progress, Plutarch's Lives, The Spectator, Xenophon: books and writers he read. The thirteen virtues: Temperance, Silence, Order, Resolution, Frugality, Industry, Sincerity, Justice, Moderation, Cleanliness, Tranquillity, Chastity, Humility. Places: Boston, Ecton, New York, Perth Amboy, Burlington, Philadelphia, London, Pennsylvania, Albany, Lancaster, Twyford, Delaware, Market Street. Key terms: Apprentice, Tallow, Almanack, Printing press, Newspaper, Vegetarian, Junto, Subscription, Militia, Lightning, Dissertation, Indenture, Sloop. Voice and tone: first person told simply in third person for learners, warm, wry and honest; Franklin laughs at his own faults; the writer admires his curiosity and his habit of improving himself.

beats.scene: A man writes a letter by a window in a quiet English house
beats.summary: In 1771 Franklin begins to write the story of his life as a letter to his son William.

beats.scene: An old stone village in the English countryside with a church and farms
beats.summary: Franklin traces his family back to the village of Ecton, where they were smiths and small farmers for about three hundred years.

beats.scene: A crowded wooden house in Boston with many children at a table
beats.summary: Josiah Franklin moves to Boston; Benjamin, born in January 1706, is the youngest son of a large family of seventeen children.

beats.scene: A small boy in a plain schoolroom stands in front of a teacher
beats.summary: At eight Benjamin goes to grammar school, then to a school for writing and sums, and leaves school at ten.

beats.scene: A boy in an apron cuts thread for candles in a busy workshop
beats.summary: Josiah makes candles and soap; Benjamin works in the shop cutting wicks, hates it, and longs for the sea, so his father walks him round the town to see other trades.

beats.scene: A boy sits on the floor with an open book in a crowded room
beats.summary: Benjamin spends every penny on books, and reads Bunyan, Plutarch and Defoe among others.

beats.scene: A boy of twelve signs a paper beside a wooden printing press
beats.summary: At twelve Benjamin becomes an apprentice in his brother James's print shop, bound until he is twenty-one.

beats.scene: Benjamin reads by candlelight at night while a street song-seller stands outside
beats.summary: He borrows books at night from a bookseller's customer, and writes two ballads that his brother has him sell in the streets.

beats.scene: Two boys argue earnestly across a table while a father reads a page
beats.summary: In an argument by letter with his friend John Collins, Benjamin sees from his father's remarks that his writing needs work.

beats.scene: A teenage boy copies out a magazine essay at night by candlelight
beats.summary: Benjamin finds a volume of The Spectator, studies it, and practises by rewriting its ideas in his own words, turning them into verse and back.

beats.scene: A young man eats bread and raisins at a printing desk
beats.summary: At sixteen he reads a book on vegetable eating, stops eating meat, and saves half his food money for books.

beats.scene: A young man questions an older friend politely in a quiet room
beats.summary: Reading about Socrates, he learns to ask polite questions instead of arguing, and to say I think rather than it is certain.

beats.scene: James Franklin and young men stand at a printing press with a newspaper sheet
beats.summary: In 1721 James begins a newspaper, the New-England Courant; some friends say one paper is enough for the town.

beats.scene: A young man pushes a folded letter under a printing-house door at night
beats.summary: Benjamin secretly writes letters in the name of a widow, Silence Dogood, and slips them under the door; they are admired.

beats.scene: James Franklin sits in a prison cell while Benjamin works the press alone
beats.summary: James is jailed for a month in 1722 for upsetting the government; Benjamin runs the paper, and it is then printed under his name.

beats.scene: Two brothers argue in a print shop and one raises his hand
beats.summary: The brothers quarrel, James strikes him, and Benjamin decides to leave Boston, though he has a contract.

beats.scene: A small sailing boat leaves Boston harbour at dawn with a young passenger
beats.summary: Benjamin sells some of his books for money and boards a sloop to New York at seventeen, with a friend's help, in 1723.

beats.scene: A small boat crosses a stormy river as a man leans over the side
beats.summary: No work in New York; the printer Bradford sends him on to Philadelphia. The boat is blown about in a storm, and he pulls a drunken passenger from the water.

beats.scene: A tired young man in dirty clothes walks up a street with bread rolls
beats.summary: He arrives in Philadelphia on a Sunday morning, dirty and tired, buys three rolls with almost all his money, and a girl, Deborah Read, laughs at him.

beats.scene: A printing shop with an old press and a thin man at a desk
beats.summary: He finds work with a printer, Samuel Keimer, whose press is old and who writes directly into type, and lodges with the Read family.

beats.scene: A gentleman in a long coat visits a small print shop
beats.summary: Governor Sir William Keith hears of the clever apprentice, visits him, and offers to help him set up his own printing business.

beats.scene: A father reads a letter in a Boston home while his son waits
beats.summary: Benjamin returns to Boston to ask his father for money to set up a business; Josiah thinks he is too young and says no, but gives his blessing.

beats.scene: A ship crosses the grey Atlantic with two young men on deck
beats.summary: Governor Keith promises letters of credit for London, and Benjamin sails there with his friend James Ralph in 1724; the letters never come.

beats.scene: Two young men look at crowded London streets with their bags
beats.summary: In London with no money, Ralph borrows from Franklin and does not repay; Franklin finds a job in a printing house.

beats.scene: A young printer carries two heavy trays of type upstairs past beer drinkers
beats.summary: In a London print shop the workers drink beer all day; Franklin drinks water and carries heavier loads, and they call him the Water-American.

beats.scene: A kind merchant in a long coat speaks to Benjamin in a busy shop
beats.summary: A Quaker merchant, Thomas Denham, offers him a job as a clerk in Philadelphia; Franklin sails home in 1726 after about eighteen months.

beats.scene: A sick man lies in bed while a friend sits beside him
beats.summary: Franklin and Denham both fall ill; Denham dies, and Franklin, with no master, goes back to work for Keimer.

beats.scene: Two young printers unpack a new press in a small rented shop
beats.summary: Franklin and his friend Hugh Meredith set up their own printing business, with Meredith's father's help.

beats.scene: Young men talk around a table in a tavern in the evening
beats.summary: In 1727 Franklin forms the Junto, a club of friends who meet on Friday evenings to discuss morals, politics and science and help each other.

beats.scene: A printer and a customer exchange papers across a desk
beats.summary: He writes a pamphlet on paper money, wins the government's printing work, and buys the Pennsylvania Gazette from Keimer in 1729.

beats.scene: A young man pushes a wheelbarrow of paper through a street at dawn
beats.summary: To win trust, Franklin lives plainly and is seen working hard, even wheeling paper through the street on a barrow.

beats.scene: A smiling couple sort pamphlets together in a small shop
beats.summary: In 1730 Franklin marries Deborah Read, whose husband had left; she helps in the shop and they live frugally.

beats.scene: People carry books into a small room where they place them on shelves
beats.summary: In 1731 Franklin proposes a subscription library: each member pays to join, and all may borrow; he keeps his own name out of it.

beats.scene: A printer sits at a desk beside a stack of almanacs by lamplight
beats.summary: From 1732 he prints Poor Richard's Almanack, full of jokes and savings sayings, which sells about ten thousand copies a year.

beats.scene: A thoughtful young man writes in a small notebook by candlelight
beats.summary: Around 1730 Franklin forms the bold plan of becoming a morally perfect person, and finds it harder than expected.

beats.scene: A list of thirteen words written in neat columns in a small book
beats.summary: He lists thirteen virtues to practise: temperance, silence, order, resolution, frugality, industry, sincerity, justice, moderation, cleanliness, tranquillity, chastity and humility.

beats.scene: A small notebook with red lines and small black marks beside a pen
beats.summary: He keeps a little book with a page for each virtue and marks every fault with a black spot, working on one virtue each week.

beats.scene: A neat desk with papers in order beside a man holding a speckled axe
beats.summary: Order is hardest for him; he tells how a man wanted his axe polished all over, and chose a speckled one, saying it was good enough.

beats.scene: A man bows his head slightly while another man speaks with confidence
beats.summary: Pride is the hardest fault to beat; he says that if he thought he had beaten it, he would probably be proud of his humility, and he softens his speech.

beats.scene: A man sits quietly at a plain wooden table with an open book
beats.summary: On religion he holds a simple creed: there is one God, who should be served by doing good to others; and he tells people to judge by deeds.

beats.scene: A vast crowd in a Philadelphia street listens to a preacher
beats.summary: In 1739 the preacher George Whitefield draws huge crowds; Franklin decides not to give but ends up emptying his pockets, and works out that thirty thousand might hear him.

beats.scene: A clerk writes by candlelight and a postman rides away on a horse
beats.summary: He becomes clerk of the Assembly in 1736 and postmaster of Philadelphia in 1737, and improves the night watch and starts the first fire company.

beats.scene: Workers sweep and pave a muddy market street while lamps are lit above
beats.summary: He helps to get streets paved and swept and designs better street lamps, whose glass stays clear.

beats.scene: Many men sign a long paper at tables set up in a hall
beats.summary: In 1747, when war threatens, he writes Plain Truth and organises a volunteer force; over ten thousand sign, and they raise money with a lottery.

beats.scene: A man holds a glass tube near sparks beside an iron stove
beats.summary: He invents a stove that gives more heat for less wood, and refuses to take a patent; he also does experiments on electricity.

beats.scene: A group of men and women stand outside a new hospital and academy building
beats.summary: He helps to found the Academy of Philadelphia in 1749 and, with Dr Bond, the Pennsylvania Hospital in 1751, persuading the Assembly to match donations.

beats.scene: Delegates sit around a long table at Albany with a map
beats.summary: In 1754 Franklin goes to Albany and proposes a plan to unite the colonies; the delegates approve it, but neither the colonies nor the Crown accept it.

beats.scene: A long line of farm wagons with horses stands on a dusty road
beats.summary: In 1755 Franklin finds wagons and horses for General Braddock's army, offering to pay the farmers himself; Braddock is later defeated.

beats.scene: A ship sails out of a harbour with a man at the rail
beats.summary: In 1757 the Assembly sends him to London to argue with the Penn family about taxes; he sets sail, and the story is left at this point.

beats.scene: An old man with white hair sits at a desk among papers
beats.summary: The book stops in 1757; Franklin lived until 1790, and helped to shape a new nation, but he left his own story unfinished.

A1A2: In 1771, Benjamin Franklin began to write his life story for his son.
His family came from a small village in England called Ecton.
Benjamin was born in Boston in 1706, the youngest son in a big family.
At eight, Benjamin went to school, but he left when he was ten.
Benjamin helped in his father's shop, where they made candles and soap.
Benjamin loved to read, and he spent all his small coins on books.
At twelve, he began to work for his brother James, a printer.
At night, he read books that a friend lent him.
His father read his letters and said that his writing was weak.
He found a book of fine essays and learned to write from it.
At sixteen, he stopped eating meat and saved money for books.
He learned that polite questions work better than angry arguments.
In 1721, James began to print a new newspaper in Boston.
Benjamin secretly wrote letters and put them under the shop door.
In 1722, James went to prison, and Benjamin ran the newspaper.
The brothers fought, and Benjamin decided that he must leave.
He sold some books, and sailed away on a small boat.
In New York, there was no work, so he went on to Philadelphia.
He came to Philadelphia tired and dirty, with very little money.
He found work with a printer, and lived in the Read house.
A powerful man offered to help Benjamin start his own business.
He asked his father for money, but his father said no.
The governor promised letters, so Benjamin sailed for London.
In London, he had little money, so he looked for work.
The other workers drank beer, but Benjamin only drank water.
A kind merchant offered him a job in Philadelphia, so he went home.
Both men became sick, and Mr Denham died, so Benjamin lost his job.
With his friend Hugh Meredith, he opened his own printing shop.
In 1727, Benjamin started a club of friends who met on Fridays.
In 1729, he bought a newspaper and made it much better.
He worked very hard, and people could see that he did.
In 1730, Benjamin married Deborah Read, and she helped in the shop.
In 1731, Benjamin started a library that many people could use.
In 1732, he began to print Poor Richard's Almanack each year.
Benjamin made a plan to become a better person every day.
He chose thirteen good habits, such as order, honesty and hard work.
He kept a small book and marked each mistake with a spot.
He found it very hard to keep his papers in good order.
He said that pride was the hardest fault to defeat.
He believed that doing good to other people was the best service.
In 1739, a famous preacher came, and Benjamin gave all his money.
Benjamin took on public jobs and helped to make the town safer.
He helped to get the streets of the city paved and cleaned.
In 1747, he helped to form an army of volunteers for defence.
He invented a better stove but did not ask for any payment.
He also helped to start a school and a hospital.
In 1754, he proposed a plan to unite the colonies.
He found many wagons and horses for the army of General Braddock.
In 1757, Benjamin sailed to London to speak for Pennsylvania.
He lived until 1790, but he never finished his story.
B1B2: In 1771, Benjamin Franklin sat down in a quiet English country house and began a letter to his son William. He wanted to tell his family how a poor boy had become a successful man.
The Franklin family had lived in the village of Ecton for at least three hundred years. Many of them were blacksmiths, and they also worked a small piece of land.
Benjamin's father, Josiah, had sailed to Boston from England with his wife and children. Benjamin was born there in January 1706, and he was the youngest son among seventeen children.
His father hoped that Benjamin would become a minister, so he sent him to school at the age of eight. The cost was too high, however, and Benjamin left school when he was only ten.
Josiah made candles and soap, and Benjamin had to cut the thread for the candles and fill the moulds. He disliked the work and dreamed of the sea, so Josiah took him to watch other trades.
As a boy, Benjamin spent every penny he had on books. He read the stories of Bunyan and the lives of famous Greeks and Romans by Plutarch, and he never forgot them.
When Benjamin was twelve, he signed a paper to work for his older brother James, who had just opened a print shop. He would be an apprentice until the age of twenty-one.

A friend who worked for a bookseller lent him books, and Benjamin read them at night and returned them in the morning. He also wrote two songs, and his brother sent him out to sell them in the streets.

Benjamin and his friend John Collins argued by letter about whether women should be taught as well as men. Josiah read the letters, and he told his son that the spelling was good, but the writing was not clear.

He found a volume of The Spectator, a famous collection of essays, and he thought the writing was excellent. He made notes about each essay, and later he tried to write it again, even turning some into poems and back.
When he was sixteen, he read a book that said it was wrong to eat meat, so he decided to stop. He asked his brother to give him half of the food money, and he spent it on books.

He read about the Greek thinker Socrates, who asked questions instead of making arguments. Benjamin learned to use words like I think and it seems to me, and he found that people listened to him more.
In 1721, James started a newspaper called the New-England Courant. Some of his friends thought that Boston did not need another newspaper, but he went ahead.
Benjamin wished to write for the newspaper, but he knew his brother would refuse. So he made up a widow named Silence Dogood, and he slid her letters under the door at night.
In 1722, James was put in prison for a month, because the newspaper had upset the government. Benjamin ran the paper alone, and after that it was printed in his name.
The two brothers quarrelled often, and James sometimes hit him. Benjamin decided that he could not stay in Boston, and he took advantage of the fact that his old contract had been given back.
Benjamin sold some of his books to pay for the journey, and a friend helped him to board a small ship. He was seventeen years old, and nobody in his family knew where he was going.
The printer in New York had no job for him, so he told Benjamin to try Philadelphia. The trip took a long time, because a storm blew the boat off course.
Benjamin arrived on a Sunday morning, hungry and dirty, with only a Dutch dollar and a few pennies. He bought three large rolls and walked up Market Street with one under each arm, eating the third.
He soon found a job with a printer named Samuel Keimer, who had an old press and little skill. Benjamin also found a room in the home of Mr Read, the father of the girl who had laughed at him.
The governor of Pennsylvania, Sir William Keith, heard about the clever young printer and came to meet him. He promised to help Benjamin open a print shop of his own.
Benjamin went back to Boston to ask his father for money to start a business. Josiah said that he was too young for such a heavy responsibility, but he was glad to see his son again.
Governor Keith said he would send letters to help him buy a printing press in London. Benjamin sailed there with his friend James Ralph, but on the ship he found that no letters had been sent.
Benjamin and Ralph arrived in London with little money, and Ralph soon spent most of Benjamin's. Benjamin found work in a printing house, where he did his job well.

The other workers in the print shop drank a lot of beer, but Benjamin drank water. He could carry two heavy trays of type up the stairs, while they carried only one, so they called him the Water-American.
A Quaker merchant named Thomas Denham offered Benjamin a job in his shop in Philadelphia. In July 1726, after about eighteen months in London, Benjamin sailed home.
Benjamin and Mr Denham both became very ill, and sadly Mr Denham died. Benjamin was left without a master, so he went back to work for Keimer.
After a quarrel with Keimer, Benjamin started his own business with his friend Hugh Meredith. Hugh's father paid for the press and the type.
In 1727, Benjamin formed a club of friends that he called the Junto. They met on Friday evenings to talk about morals, politics and science, and to help each other.
Benjamin wrote a pamphlet about paper money, which helped him to win government printing work. In 1729, he bought a newspaper called the Pennsylvania Gazette from Keimer.

Benjamin knew that a young businessman must be trusted, so he dressed plainly and avoided fun that wasted time. He even pushed paper through the streets on a wheelbarrow, so that everyone could see how hard he worked.
In 1730, Benjamin married Deborah Read, whose first husband had left her years before. She worked in the shop, folding pamphlets and watching the money, and she helped the business grow.
Books were expensive, and few people could afford many. In 1731, Benjamin suggested that members should each pay a small fee to start one library for all.
In 1732, Benjamin began to print a yearly book called Poor Richard's Almanack. It was full of jokes, weather notes and wise sayings, and it sold about ten thousand copies each year.
Benjamin made a bold plan to live without making any mistakes. He soon found that it was much harder than he had expected, because bad habits kept coming back.
Benjamin made a list of thirteen virtues, including temperance, order, industry, sincerity and justice. He explained each one with a short rule, and he planned to practise them one at a time.
Benjamin kept a little book with a page for each virtue, and he marked every mistake with a black spot. He worked on one virtue each week, and in a year he could go through all thirteen four times.
Of all the virtues, Benjamin found order the hardest. He tells a story of a man who wanted a bright axe, but who finally preferred a speckled one, because it was easier to keep.
Pride, he said, was the hardest fault to beat. If he ever believed that he had conquered it, he joked, he would probably be proud of his humility.
Benjamin believed in one God, and he thought that the best way to serve Him was by doing good to other people. He did not often go to church, but he respected people of all faiths.
In 1739, the preacher George Whitefield drew huge crowds in Philadelphia. Benjamin had decided not to give any money, but as he listened, he emptied all of his pockets.
In 1736, Benjamin became clerk of the Pennsylvania Assembly, and in 1737 he became the postmaster of Philadelphia. He also helped to improve the night watch and to start a fire company.
Philadelphia's streets were covered in mud, so Benjamin helped to arrange for them to be paved and swept. He also designed better street lamps, which did not turn black with smoke.
In 1747, war threatened Pennsylvania, and the colony had no army. Benjamin wrote a pamphlet called Plain Truth, and more than ten thousand men signed up to defend their homes.
Benjamin invented an iron stove that gave more heat while using less wood. He did not take out a patent, because he thought that people should share their good ideas.
In 1749, Benjamin helped to start a school, which later became the University of Pennsylvania. With his friend Dr Bond, he also helped to open a hospital in 1751.
In 1754, Benjamin went to Albany to meet delegates from several colonies. He proposed a plan to unite them, and the delegates approved it, but the assemblies and the king's ministers did not.
In 1755, General Braddock's army needed wagons to march into the wilderness. Benjamin gathered about a hundred and fifty wagons from the farmers, and he promised to pay them if the army did not.
In 1757, the Assembly sent Benjamin to England, because the Penn family, who owned the colony, would not pay their share of the taxes. He sailed from New York in April to speak for Pennsylvania.
Franklin wrote his book in several parts and never finished it, and the story stops in 1757. He lived until 1790, when he died at the age of eighty-four.
C1C2: In the summer of 1771, Benjamin Franklin was staying in a quiet English country house, far from the noise of London politics, when he began a long letter addressed to his son William. He explained that old men like to talk about their past, and that his descendants might enjoy learning how a humble boy had risen in the world. The pages that followed would grow into one of the most famous life stories ever written, although Franklin himself never finished it.

Franklin tells us that his family had lived in the English village of Ecton for at least three hundred years, long before anyone thought of writing their names down. Most of the men worked as blacksmiths, and they also farmed a small piece of land that passed from father to son. He had collected these stories from an old uncle, and he repeated them because he thought a family ought to remember where it began.

Josiah Franklin had crossed the Atlantic to Boston in search of a freer life, and there he raised a family so large that his table was seldom empty. Benjamin was born in January 1706 and was the youngest son among seventeen children, by two wives. His mother, Abiah Folger, was the second of those wives, and Franklin remembered her as a sensible woman who fed her large family well.

Josiah wanted his youngest son to become a minister, so he sent Benjamin to a grammar school at the age of eight, where the boy did very well. The fees were too high for a large family, though, and after a short time he was moved to a school that taught only writing and arithmetic. By the time he was ten, his schooling had ended, and everything else he learned he would have to teach himself.

At ten years old Benjamin joined his father's shop, where Josiah boiled fat to make candles and soap, and the boy spent his days cutting wicks and filling the moulds. He found the work dull and smelly, and his heart was set on a life at sea, so Josiah took him on walks round Boston to watch bricklayers, carpenters and other craftsmen at work. The boy loved to see skilled hands, but in the end it was his love of books that decided his future.

From the time he could read, Benjamin used every penny he earned to buy small books, and he later sold some of them in order to buy others. He read John Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress, the lives of great Greeks and Romans by Plutarch, and an essay by Daniel Defoe that taught him to think about how to improve a town. Franklin believed that these early books, more than anything else, shaped the way he looked at the world.

James Franklin had come home from England with a printing press and a set of type, and Josiah agreed that his youngest son should learn the trade from him. At the age of twelve, Benjamin signed a contract that bound him to his brother as an apprentice for nine years, with proper wages only in the last of them. Franklin admits that he soon became skilful, and that he was sad to see how quickly his brother began to treat him as a servant rather than as a brother.

Printing gave Benjamin the chance to meet people who owned books, and one of them, a customer named Matthew Adams, let him borrow from his fine library. The young apprentice often sat up half the night reading, so that he could give each volume back by morning before it was missed. He also wrote two songs about sailors and pirates, and James had him sell them in the streets, but his father laughed at the verses and told him that poets are generally poor.

Benjamin loved a good argument, and he and his friend John Collins once spent weeks debating by letter whether women should be given the same education as men. Josiah happened to read the pages, and he gently told his son that although the spelling and the printing were fine, his writing was weak in style, order and clarity. The criticism hurt, but it was fair, and it made Benjamin determined to learn to write well.

One day Benjamin came across a volume of the Spectator, a collection of elegant essays, and he admired the clear and polished way in which they were written. He made brief notes about each piece, put them aside for a few days, and then tried to rebuild the essay in his own words before comparing it with the original. He even turned some essays into verse, and back again, so that he had to search for new words, and slowly he came to see where his own faults lay.

At sixteen, Benjamin read a book arguing that eating meat was cruel and unhealthy, and he decided at once to give it up, which caused some trouble in his brother's house. He offered to feed himself on half of the money that James paid for his food, and then bought books with the savings, living cheaply on bread, a handful of raisins and a glass of water. This meant he finished his meals quickly, leaving him more time to read while the others were still eating.

In a book about the Greek philosopher Socrates, the young printer discovered a better way to argue: ask humble questions, and let the other person find the weak point in his own idea. He gave up sharp words such as certainly and undoubtedly, and used softer phrases like I think or it seems to me, which made people far more willing to listen. Franklin noticed that a person who corrects others too bluntly may be right, but he rarely wins their hearts.

In 1721 James Franklin decided to start a newspaper, which he called the New-England Courant, and Benjamin helped to set the type and then carried the printed sheets round the town to the customers. Some of James's friends warned him that Boston had enough newspapers already and that the new one would probably fail. It did not, and it turned out to be bolder and livelier than anything the town had seen before.

Benjamin longed to write for the Courant, but he feared that James would never print the words of a mere apprentice, so he invented a clever widow named Silence Dogood. In a disguised hand he wrote her letters, and one night he slipped them under the print-shop door, where James and his friends found them in the morning. The readers praised the new writer and tried to guess who it might be, and when Benjamin finally told the truth, his brother was not pleased.

The Courant soon angered the leaders of Massachusetts, and in 1722 James was sent to prison for a month after printing something that offended the government. Benjamin kept the newspaper going by himself, and when James was ordered to stop publishing altogether, the paper was printed under Benjamin's name instead. To make this look proper, his old contract was given back to him, though he secretly signed a new one, a trick that he later admitted was not entirely honest.

Relations between the brothers grew steadily worse, as James was proud and hot-tempered, and he sometimes struck his young apprentice in anger, which Benjamin never forgave. Because his old contract had been returned, Benjamin realised that he could leave in secret, and he knew that James could not prove the new one in court. Looking back, Franklin called this act of leaving one of the first mistakes of his life, but he also admitted that his brother had treated him harshly.

With a little money from the sale of some books, and with the help of his friend John Collins, Benjamin slipped aboard a sloop that was sailing for New York. He was only seventeen, he had no friends there, and his family had no idea where he had gone, which he regretted later. After three days at sea he stepped ashore in a strange city, nearly three hundred miles from his home, and began to look for work.

The printer William Bradford had no work to offer, but he told Benjamin that his son in Philadelphia might need a helper, and so the young traveller took a boat across the bay. A storm drove them off course, and in the middle of it a drunken Dutchman fell overboard, whom Benjamin pulled back aboard by the hair and who was soaked but safe. After a long, wet journey, partly on foot, he finally came to the river at Philadelphia.

Benjamin stepped off the boat in Philadelphia early on a Sunday morning, with dirty clothes, empty pockets and nothing in them but a Dutch dollar and a handful of copper coins. He bought three large puffy rolls, tucked one under each arm and ate the third as he walked up Market Street, looking, as he admits, quite ridiculous. A young woman named Deborah Read stood at her father's door and laughed at the sight, and years later she became his wife.

Within days Benjamin had found work with Samuel Keimer, a strange and rather clumsy printer who owned an old press and composed his poems straight into metal type without writing them first. The young man took lodgings in the house of Mr Read, and since he was quiet, clean and hard-working, he soon earned the family's respect. It was a modest start, but after months of danger and hunger it felt like the beginning of a new life.

Word of the gifted young printer reached the governor, Sir William Keith, who surprised everyone by visiting Keimer's shop in person to speak with Benjamin. He praised the young man's talent, told him that the town needed a good printer, and promised to use his influence to win him the government's printing contracts. Benjamin, flattered and trusting, believed every word of it, though he did not yet know the governor's reputation.

Keith insisted that the plan would only work with Josiah's support, so Benjamin travelled back to Boston, where he was welcomed home by a family that had long feared for him. His father read the governor's letter carefully, praised his son's progress, and then declined to lend him the money, saying that at eighteen he was still too young to take such a heavy responsibility. Benjamin returned to Philadelphia with his father's blessing, a few presents, and no money for the business at all.

Not discouraged, Keith promised to give Benjamin letters of credit that would allow him to buy a press and type in London, and in November 1724 the young man sailed across the Atlantic with his poetical friend James Ralph. When he asked for the letters, however, the ship's captain found none, and a fellow passenger told him that the governor was famous for promising everything and doing nothing. Benjamin later wrote that he was shocked, but that he had learned an important lesson about trusting people who make large promises.

London in 1725 was enormous, crowded and expensive, and the two friends soon found that their small savings would not last long. Ralph spent most of Benjamin's money on theatres and his own comfort and never repaid it, while Benjamin found regular work at a large printing house, and refused to join his friend in the pleasures of the town. He remained there for almost a year, learning new skills and slowly building his savings.

In the London printing house, the workmen drank beer all day long, beginning with a pint at breakfast, and they teased Benjamin because he drank only water. He proved that water was good enough for anyone by carrying two heavy forms of type up and down the stairs at once, while the beer drinkers needed both hands for one. They nicknamed him the Water-American, and he noted with some satisfaction that several of them eventually gave up the habit.

Thomas Denham, a Quaker merchant who had crossed the sea with Benjamin on the outward journey, offered to take him back to Philadelphia as a clerk and to teach him the business of trade. Benjamin accepted gladly, left his London friends and sailed home in July 1726 after about eighteen months abroad. He found, on his return, that Deborah Read had married someone else, and he later admitted that he had written to her only once, which he considered a serious mistake.

Soon after their return, both Benjamin and his master fell seriously ill, and Benjamin was so weak that he almost hoped to die, but he recovered. Mr Denham was not so fortunate, and his death left the young man without a patron, a future or a position, so he drifted back to Samuel Keimer's shop. Keimer offered him good wages to manage the press and to train his apprentices, and Benjamin, with few choices, agreed.

After a disagreement with Keimer, Benjamin left and formed a partnership with his friend Hugh Meredith, whose father was happy to pay for a press and the type to go with it. They set up business in a small rented shop in Philadelphia, though Meredith was fond of drink and proved to be a rather weak partner. Eventually two loyal friends, William Coleman and Robert Grace, lent Benjamin the money to buy Meredith out and carry on alone.

In the autumn of 1727 Benjamin gathered a dozen of his cleverest friends into a club that he called the Junto, and they met on Friday evenings to debate questions of morals, politics and natural science. Each member took a turn to bring a question for discussion, and the rules were designed to keep the talk friendly, since the aim was to find the truth rather than to win the argument. The club lasted nearly forty years, and Franklin was convinced that it did more good for the town than any single member could have done alone.

In 1729 Benjamin wrote a small pamphlet defending the use of paper money, and the argument pleased the leaders of the colony so much that they gave him the printing of the money itself. The same year he bought Keimer's struggling newspaper, renamed it the Pennsylvania Gazette, and improved it with lively essays, useful news and carefully chosen advertisements. Within a few years it became the most successful newspaper in the colonies, and Franklin was well on his way to being comfortably wealthy.

Benjamin understood that credit depends on reputation, so he took care to appear industrious as well as to be so, dressing simply, avoiding taverns and refusing every amusement that might waste his hours. He even wheeled rolls of paper through the streets on a barrow, since the neighbours who saw him would naturally conclude that the young printer was a man to be trusted. Franklin confessed that appearances mattered a great deal, but that the hard work behind them had to be real.

In September 1730 Benjamin took Deborah Read as his wife; her first husband had left the country and was reported to have died, so there was some uncertainty about the law. Deborah proved an excellent partner, for she folded pamphlets, kept the shop, bought old linen rags for the paper-makers and managed the household with great care. Franklin remembered that they both kept to a simple style of living, and that frugal habits had done much to secure their prosperity.

Books were rare and costly in the colonies, and Benjamin saw that readers could achieve together what none could do alone, by each paying a modest sum into a shared collection. In 1731 about fifty subscribers founded the Library Company, and members could borrow volumes freely for a small yearly payment. Franklin deliberately presented the idea as the plan of a group of friends, because he had noticed that people resist a scheme that makes one man look clever.

In 1732 Franklin began publishing Poor Richard's Almanack, a yearly book of weather forecasts, jokes and rhymes that he made both entertaining and useful for ordinary readers. Between the pages he scattered short sayings that urged people to be careful with money, such as the remark that an empty bag cannot stand upright, and the book sold about ten thousand copies each year. It brought him both profit and fame, and he continued to write it for twenty-five years.

Not content with success in business, Benjamin formed what he called a bold and difficult plan: to live every moment without committing any fault, and to reach moral perfection. He discovered quickly that the task was harder than he had imagined, for while he was guarding against one mistake, he would often fall into another. He decided that good intentions were not enough, and that he needed a method, so he sat down to find one.

After careful thought, Franklin listed thirteen virtues that he hoped to master: temperance, silence, order, resolution, frugality, industry, sincerity, justice, moderation, cleanliness, tranquillity, chastity and humility. Beside each one he wrote a short rule that explained exactly what it meant, such as eating not to dullness or drinking not to excess. He decided to work on them one by one, believing that once one habit was established, the next would be easier to win.

Franklin kept a small book with a page for each virtue, ruled in red ink so that he could mark each fault in the correct column with a black spot at the end of every day. He concentrated on one virtue each week, which meant that he could complete the full cycle of thirteen weeks four times in a single year. His aim was to see the pages grow cleaner, and he found that the book kept him honest in a way that vague good intentions never could.

Of all the virtues, order proved the hardest for Benjamin, because a busy printer's papers and tools seemed always to end up in the wrong place. He recalled a man who asked a smith to polish his axe until it shone all over, and who gave up halfway, saying that he liked a speckled axe best. Franklin admitted that many of us give up on perfection in the same way, and that a speckled character may be good enough for an ordinary person.

Franklin wrote that of all the natural passions, pride was the most difficult to subdue, because even when it was hidden it lived on beneath the surface, ready to creep back. He joked that if he believed he had finally overcome it, he would no doubt feel proud of his humility, and that he had come to accept that perfection was beyond him. Still, he said, he was a better and happier man for having made the attempt, and for avoiding the habit of correcting people in a haughty tone.

On matters of religion Franklin held a simple creed, that one God made the world and that the best service we can offer Him is to do good to our fellow men. He rarely attended church, and found the sermons of his day dull, but he gave money to every congregation that asked and respected every honest believer. What mattered to him, he said, was not what a person claimed to believe, but how that person behaved.

When the preacher George Whitefield came to Philadelphia in 1739, he drew crowds so large that no church could hold them, and Franklin went to hear him out of curiosity. Having privately decided not to give a penny, he found himself so moved that he emptied his pocket of copper, then silver and finally gold into the collection. Afterwards he walked to the edge of the crowd and calculated from the distance at which he could still hear the voice that more than thirty thousand people might hear a speaker in the open air.

As his business prospered, Benjamin was chosen as clerk of the Pennsylvania Assembly in 1736 and as postmaster of Philadelphia the following year, and each office gave him more influence and more chances to be useful. He wrote a paper that persuaded the town to pay for a better night watch, and he organised a volunteer fire company in which neighbours promised to help each other with buckets and bags. His fellow citizens were so pleased with the fire company that other groups were soon formed in imitation.

In wet weather the streets of Philadelphia became rivers of mud, and Franklin wrote a paper showing how paving the market and sweeping the streets could improve the health and the trade of the whole town. He also noticed that the globe lamps in use were soon blackened by smoke, and so he designed a new lamp with four flat panes and a chimney, which stayed clearer and burned more brightly. Whenever he saw a problem, it seems, his instinct was to design a practical solution.

In 1747, with enemy ships lurking in the Delaware river and no army in Pennsylvania, Franklin wrote a pamphlet entitled Plain Truth that urged ordinary citizens to unite and defend themselves. Within weeks, more than ten thousand men had signed their names to a plan for a volunteer militia, and the town raised money for cannon by holding a public lottery. Franklin noted with quiet pride that none of this was done by order of government, but by ordinary people deciding to help themselves.

Around 1742 Franklin designed an iron fireplace that gave out far more heat while burning much less wood, and the governor offered him a patent which would have earned him a fortune. He refused, explaining that since we all enjoy great advantages from the inventions of other people, we should be happy to serve others by any invention of our own, and that we should do so freely. In the following years he turned to electricity, and his experiments with sparks and lightning would make him famous across Europe, though he treats them lightly in this book.

Franklin believed that a young country needed good schools, and in 1749 he published a plan for an academy that later grew into the University of Pennsylvania. Two years later he helped his friend Dr Thomas Bond to found a hospital for the poor, and he persuaded the Assembly to promise a sum of money if private citizens first raised an equal amount. It was a clever way of making people give, and it worked so well that the hospital was soon opened.

In the summer of 1754 Franklin travelled to Albany as a delegate to a conference of the colonies, and there he put forward a plan under which they would join together in a single government for defence and other common needs. The delegates approved it, but the colonial assemblies thought it gave too much power to the Crown, while in London it was judged to give too much to the people. Franklin concluded that if both sides disliked it, the plan must have been fairly balanced.

When General Braddock arrived in 1755 to lead an army against the French, his men could not move for lack of wagons, until Franklin offered to find some by writing to the farmers of Pennsylvania. He promised in his own name to pay for any wagon that was lost, and in a short time about a hundred and fifty wagons and hundreds of horses were on their way. Braddock was defeated in the woods soon after, and Franklin, who had warned him of the danger of an ambush, had the sad satisfaction of being right.

In 1757 the Pennsylvania Assembly chose Franklin to travel to London and argue its case against the Penn family, the owners of the colony, who refused to pay a fair share of taxes. He sailed in the spring, leaving behind his wife and daughter and the newspaper he had built from nothing, and the story as he told it stops at about this point. At fifty-one he had become one of the most respected men in America, yet in many ways his greatest work was still ahead of him.

Franklin wrote his life story in several parts, at different times, and he died in 1790 at the age of eighty-four without carrying it any further than the year 1757. In the years that followed he would help to shape a new nation, serving as a scientist, a diplomat and a leader in the founding of the United States. Yet the little book he left us still shows what its author valued most, which was curiosity, hard work, honesty and a determination to make himself and the world a little better.
